newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OPEC - An ageing cartel may need a facelift.
newsitem.headline: OPEC - An ageing cartel may need a facelift.

text.p: OPEC's latest attempt to convince world oil markets that it can shore up a dilapidated quota system looks set to backfire and only hasten the day when the ageing cartel finally admits it needs a facelift.
Saudi Arabia and Iran set aside Gulf political rivalries and put their authority to the test at a conference of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries in Vienna this week.
They joined forces to put pressure on those others among the 11 members who are violating mandatory oil output limits and extract promises of better behaviour from them.

But within 24 hours of an OPEC agreement to keep quotas unchanged for six more months, and stick to them, acrimonious exchanges were reflecting divisions which go to the heart of the debate about OPEC's future.
Venezuela, in excess of its official allocation for three years, argues the entire quota system is flawed.
Its state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela says OPEC should abandon quotas and opt for a policy of maximum revenues by expanding its share of the world oil market.
Other cash-pinched, populous Third World producers like Nigeria and Algeria show no sign of reversing policies which have seen Western oil company finances boost output capacity.
"They clearly need to rearrange their cartel so that it doesn't penalise membership," said Peter Gignoux, energy desk head at brokers Smith Barney in London.
"It's a fantasy world. The quota system is a mechanism for losing their share of the market," said energy analyst Geoff Pyne at bankers UBS.
OPEC's two biggest producers remain hopeful that quotas can be used to push oil prices back where they were last year -- above $20 a barrel.
But analysts say the sceptical oil market is likely to wait in vain for firm evidence that wayward over-producers honour commitments.
"People will not believe that anything has changed until they see it," said Leo Drollas, economist at former Saudi Oil Minister Zaki Yamani's Centre for Global Energy Studies.
For a moment this week traders tinkered with the idea of taking the once mighty OPEC seriously again.
Oil prices at first ticked higher on the extended accord that left unchanged a 25.03 million barrel a day (bpd) ceiling.

OPEC Secretary General Rilwanu Lukman, announcing the deal on Wednesday, said all OPEC members had pledged to return to their official allocations, enough to take two million barrels daily from world supplies.
Oil Minister Ali Naimi of Saudi Arabia said there was "100 percent commitment" among member countries.
Cracks in the new accord didn't take long to appear.
A Gulf source told reporters that Venezuela in a closed ministerial session, confessed to producing 800,000 bpd, or 30 percent aboves its quota.
"It's a lie," responded Venezuelan Oil Minister Erwin Arrieta.
OPEC headquarters in Vienna also issued a statement denying that Arrieta had owned up to overproducing.
"Whatever good they did was wiped out by Venezuela immediately denying any overproduction," said oil analyst Michael Rothman of U.S. finance house Merrill Lynch.
The problem for OPEC's old guard is that it lacks a mechanism to compel sovereign states to honour quotas.
For most oil industry observers the days when OPEC's smaller nations stood by and allowed non-OPEC producers easy access to market share are gone.
"OPEC is addressing the new issues with old policies," said Kleinwort Benson analyst Mehdi Varzi.
- -Vienna Newsroom 431 713 2002
